about: The one roadmap: the five goals, each with its steps, dates and targets. ROADMAP.md and docs/index.html are generated from this file by python bench/bench_page.py. Every step belongs to one goal; 'part' groups steps inside a goal, 'headline' names the measures that say most about it, 'today' says in a sentence what works now, and 'try' is the commands the page shows for it. Status words: done (ran and checked), doing (being worked on), next, later. start/target/done are dates; a target is a proposal and may move, but the old one is kept in 'moved' when it does. measures are ids in coverage/measures.json.
goal: Nobody should have to think about Minecraft versions or loaders: drop a mod in, as its source folder or as its .jar, from the command line or the desktop app, pick the version and the loader you want, and get it back the same way in minutes, for any mod anyone makes. On the way there: a mod or plugin author never launches Minecraft, a modpack user never diagnoses a conflict by hand, and nobody hunts for lag by hand: point mmt at a mod and within about a minute it says what is causing the lag and the known way to make it faster, and makes the change itself wherever it can prove the mod still behaves the same. Five goals: test a mod in seconds, port it to any Minecraft version automatically, make modpacks work together, move a project between loaders and platforms, and make any mod faster. Every result is proven in the real game or on a real server.

goals.title: Test a mod in seconds
goals.intro: An author changes code and gets an answer about the mod's real behaviour in seconds, without opening Minecraft: logic tests with no game, the game's own data with no game launched, and a hidden client or a real server with a bot player when the game is needed. Commands: `fast`, `data-check`, `mixin-check`, `ui-check`, `world-check`, `mp-check`, `eval`, `reload`, `plugin-check`, `server-check`.
headline: test.edit-fast
test.behaviour-checks
goals.today: Logic tests, the game's data and real-game checks all run with no game window. Paper plugins run on a real server with a bot player.

try.say: logic tests in seconds, then the real game with no window

goals.title: Port a mod to any Minecraft version
goals.intro: One command moves a mod's source from any version to any other, forward or back, with no hand edits, and the result is checked in the real game. Every edit can be undone; what cannot be ported is named, never guessed or dropped. Commands: `port`, `explain`, `dependencies`.

goals.today: Fabric and NeoForge mods as .jar or source, any version from 1.14.4 to 26.3, in about ten seconds a jar. What comes back working is the gap: of the 150 most-downloaded mods of the most-used release (Fabric 1.20.1, NeoForge 1.21.1), ported as jars to the newest game and linked against it, 11 of 294 link. One update at a time, 36% link across the 35 big updates and 93% across the 29 small ones (62% together). What does not link is named, never guessed. 16 of the 126 corpus ports build with no hand edits.

goals.title: Make modpacks work together
goals.intro: A pack user points mmt at an installed pack or an export and gets its conflicts found and repaired: duplicate and missing mods, blocks that place as another block, worlds that will not reopen. Every repair is reversible and checked on the pack's real server. Command: `pack-check`.
headline: pack.packs-in-game
goals.today: Forge, NeoForge, Fabric and Quilt packs from CurseForge, Modrinth and launcher instances, run on their real servers: worlds that will not open or reopen, crashes named by mod, duplicate and missing mods, blocks that place as another block. Two proven repairs.

goals.intro: The same project moved between Fabric, NeoForge, Forge, Quilt and Paper. A separate job from a version port, with separate claims.

Of 28 real corpus mods it accepts, 15 compile and load in the game after converting, 10 with the same behaviour fingerprint as the original and 6 with nothing left out. Forge, Quilt and Paper are not converted yet.

goals.title: Make any mod faster
goals.intro: Point mmt at a mod or a pack and, almost at once, get three things in this order: what is causing the lag (which mod, which feature, which method, and what it costs each tick or frame), how to make it faster (the fix that already worked on the same kind of slowness in another mod, with the gain it measured), and the fix made for you where mmt can prove the mod does exactly what it did before, only faster. The third is the one that matters most. It works like porting: an agent works out a kind of fix once and saves it as a tested rule, the tool applies it with no AI call, and the real game decides whether it stays. Commands: `perf`, `perf-optimize`.
headline: perf.auto-fixed
perf.known-fixes
perf.accepted-speedups
goals.today: The first works and the second has started; the third is not built. `mmt perf` attaches to a running game and after a 35-second capture ranks every mod and feature by CPU, server milliseconds per tick, render milliseconds per frame and memory. Its report names a known fix when the mod's slowness matches one of 14 saved patterns, which come from accepted speedups on 4 mods (Cyclic 15.7×, Simple Storage Network 5–6×, Diorama 1.6–2.2×, Pipez 1.2–1.3×). `mmt perf-optimize` proves a change is faster and behaves the same, but a person or their agent still writes the change: mmt edits no code for speed yet.

try.say: see which mod and feature is slow in a running game
prove a change you wrote is faster and behaves the same

decisions.question: What is the goal?
decisions.choice: Any version to any version, any loader to any loader; today one hop inside one loader is verified

decisions.question: Can modpack users get compatibility help?
decisions.choice: Yes: diagnose and resolve installed-pack conflicts, with reversible changes and real behavior checks; `pack-check` covers Forge packs

decisions.question: Are version and loader changes the same job?
decisions.choice: No; separate records, separate claims

decisions.question: Does a passing build prove a port?
decisions.choice: No; loader-refused jars, invisible UI and unloaded mods all passed builds

decisions.question: What counts as progress?
decisions.choice: A row in `coverage/ledger.json` with a receipt, shown on the progress page

decisions.question: What do we support, and how does a new kind of project get in?
decisions.choice: `SCOPE.md`: platforms by side, a six-rung support ladder, intake through the `bench-new-mod` skill

decisions.question: Plugin ↔ mod conversion?
decisions.choice: Not for now; it's a rewrite, not a port, and hybrid servers already exist. Replaced on 2026-11-09

decisions.question: Ports between Paper versions?
decisions.choice: Yes, as rung 5 for Paper once rungs 2–3 land

decisions.question: Where do roadmap steps, targets and every number we show live?
decisions.choice: `coverage/roadmap.json` (steps, dates, targets) and `coverage/measures.json` (every number, with its history and target); ROADMAP.md and the roadmap page are generated from them

decisions.question: How cheap should a game check be?
decisions.choice: 5 CPU-s per check, from 49. Checks that need the game's data but not a picture stop launching the game: data-check runs the game's own code with no window and no world (Jon, 2026-11-07, instead of sharing one started game). Picture checks keep the hidden client, with graphics settings as they are

decisions.question: Do speed targets drive work?
decisions.choice: Only when they move the goal. Phase 7 closed on Nov 7 once checks were hidden, data-check skipped the game and 8 checks ran at once; the start, cold-check, screen-check, server and pack-check speed targets became facts, the nightly job joined step 26 and pack-check's step joined Phase 6, and work went back to porting (Jon, 2026-11-07)

decisions.question: Run the real-game behaviour checks nightly?
decisions.choice: No. Their inputs (game, mods, Java) are pinned, so a nightly run repeats yesterday's answer; they run when a port reaches the game or the code they test changes (Jon, 2026-11-08)

decisions.question: Run CI on a schedule?
decisions.choice: No. Every input is pinned, so a scheduled run repeats the last answer: Stonecutter's nightly run failed one of its 100 jobs six nights in a row (Nov 2 to 7) with nobody looking. Slow checks run on demand when the code they test changes. The PR budget gate that failed a run over 300 s, queue time included, is gone too: a budget is not a check (Jon, 2026-11-08)

decisions.question: What are the goals, and in what order?
decisions.choice: Four (Jon, 2026-11-09): 1 test a mod in seconds, 2 port any mod to any version automatically, 3 make modpacks work together, 4 change loader or platform. The roadmap is grouped by goal, not by phase: old Phases 5 and 7 are Goal 1, Phases 1 to 3 are Goal 2, Phase 6 is Goal 3 and Phase 4 is Goal 4. Step ids did not change; steps 28 and 32 moved to Goal 2 because they are version ports

decisions.question: Is moving between mods and plugins a goal?
decisions.choice: Yes (Jon, 2026-11-09): Goal 4 covers every loader and platform, Paper included. Server-side code can be mapped between a loader's API and Bukkit's; client code and new blocks or items cannot run on a plugin server, and a port names them instead of dropping them (step 39)

decisions.question: How does the porter scale to any mod and any version?
decisions.choice: Not by rules read from compiler error text (355 of 358 rules matched on it, 320 hand-written per version step and naming scheme; a day of them moved the corpus from 10 to 15 building ports of 125). Jon asked for a step-back on 2026-11-17; a blind second opinion and OpenRewrite's and Error Prone's own files agree: resolve the game member behind every site of the mod on its own version and apply every known change in one typed pass; generate the target build from the loader's own starter project instead of patching each build script; write each redesign once per changed game part, ranked by mods freed. PR #97 holds the numbers

decisions.question: What chooses the next piece of porting or converting work?
decisions.choice: A list of what real mods use, and only after it has been checked against real builds (Jon asked on 2026-11-18 why progress was small and nothing was laid out). Three methods that day were each chosen from a list nobody had checked, and each missed: building ports from the loader's starter project freed 0 of 126 and lost 2 (PR #109); the port worklist cleared 21 ports of which 7 built, because it reads almost nothing in Fabric mods; three convert methods aimed at the 14 corpus mods that do not compile freed none of their three targets. The number to steer by is how many of the 150 most-downloaded mods have nothing left, read from their jars in a minute or two with no build (python bench/exposure.py run for porting, python bench/convert_coverage.py real for converting). The unit of work is one changed game part or one loader symbol, and the corpus sweep in the cloud is the proof at the end of a PR, never what chooses the work

decisions.question: Where is all of this going?
decisions.choice: One place where someone drops a mod in, picks the version and the loader they want, and gets it back very quickly, so nobody has to worry about versions or loaders (Jon, 2026-11-18). It has to be designed for any mod anyone can make, so nothing is made by hand for one mod, because that does not scale: the porter learns a changed part of the game once and the converter a piece of a loader's API once, and every mod that uses it is covered. Porting and converting stay separate records and claims (2026-10-24), and step 49 joins them behind one front door

decisions.question: What does someone hand over: the mod's source, or its .jar?
decisions.choice: Either (Jon, 2026-11-18): the mod's source folder, which comes back as source, or its .jar, which comes back as a .jar, through the command line and the desktop app. Until now port and convert took a source folder only, so only a mod's author could use them. Step 50 adds the .jar and comes first, because how it is done decides whether the source-based steps 44 and 47 stay as written

decisions.question: Does Forge → NeoForge get its own step, and which mod proves it?
decisions.choice: Yes (Jon, 2026-11-20): Forge → NeoForge is the next loader pair after Fabric and NeoForge, proven on DragonMine Z, whose NeoForge port is redone by hand each release. DragonMine Z joins the convert and port corpora as a test input; the rules stay general (step 19)

decisions.question: Why is the porting timeline months, and what is steered by now?
decisions.choice: Speed was never the gap: a .jar is ported in about ten seconds. The count was (Jon asked on 2026-11-20 why it would take months). The 62% headline was one update at a time, and half the updates change almost nothing; ported in one go to the newest game, 11 of 294 of the most-used releases' top mods link. And the to-do list was the reference the most mods share, which frees almost no mod: the 100 most shared freed 2. Steered by now: the jump to the newest game and the big updates (port.jar-links.newest, port.jar-links.big-updates), and the mods nearest to done as the order of work. Any mod, any version with nothing by hand is not a date on this roadmap: 53% of the broken references of a big update have no answer in the game's own code, and nobody ports arbitrary mods across one automatically. What is promised is a ported .jar in seconds with either every reference linked or the exact list of what is left

decisions.question: What is the performance work for?
decisions.choice: Three things, in Jon's words on 2026-11-21: "apply our thing to a mod and be able to almost instantly be able to tell 1. What's causing lag 2. How to optimize (insert known ways to make whatever faster) and 3. Auto optimize if possible (I really want this)". Until then performance was not a goal on this roadmap: the docs described a profiler and a way to prove a hand-written change, and PERFORMANCE.md said mmt never writes or proposes code. It is now goal 5, and the third part reverses that line: mmt makes the change itself, from saved rules with no AI call, and keeps it only when the real game shows the same behaviour and a real speedup.

decisions.question: Should porting, changing loader, testing and the lag work be built on one thing?
decisions.choice: Jon asked on 2026-11-21: "should these all use the same thing because that's what is happening… checking against the api and making it compatible, even with the performance thing it's about the right usage of the api". Mostly yes. Port, convert and the checks all ask where a mod touches the game and what that part is on the other side, and five separate readers answer it today; step 83 makes it one record every command uses. The lag work shares less: a slow spot is found by measuring the running game, and the record only names the game call it sits on.
